title: The Power Plant
principle: The power plants are called mitochondria.

t: You use up all your energy every few seconds. So why don't you stop?
Your body holds only a few seconds' worth of energy at a time. So why don't you run out?
A human holds a few seconds of usable energy at any moment, yet turns over roughly their own body weight of it per day. How?
ATP turnover in an adult is on the order of body mass per day against a standing pool of about 250 g. Reconcile those two numbers.
sub: Because you are making more the whole time. Energy is a river, not a bucket.
Because you never store much — you make it as fast as you spend it. Energy here is a flow, not a tank.
Because ATP is not a store. It is a flux, regenerated continuously at close to the rate it is consumed.
The pool is a buffer, not a reservoir. Stop regeneration and the buffer is gone in seconds — which is exactly why ischaemia kills tissue so fast.

question: What happens if you build lots and lots of power plants?
You are about to control how many power plants the cell has. What happens if you build as many as possible?
You control glucose supply and mitochondrial number. Predict the effect of maximising mitochondria.
Predict the response of net ATP to increasing mitochondrial density at fixed substrate supply.
options: There is a best number, and more than that is worse
stages.outcome: There is a best number, and more than that is worse
note: Have a guess before you try it.
Commit before you touch the sliders.
Predict before manipulating. The correction is what you will remember.
State the prediction first; anchoring is what makes the correction durable.

t: Move the sliders. Try to keep the energy bar from hitting the bottom.
Two sliders: how much food gets in, and how many power plants burn it. Keep the energy up for twenty seconds.
goal: You kept it going. Notice the bar never sat still — it never does.
Held steady. Notice the line never flattens: the cell is spending and remaking the whole time.

t: Each power plant costs something to run, and partway through the demand goes up. Find the setting that survives the change — not just the one that works now.
Mitochondria carry their own maintenance cost, and demand steps up at twelve seconds. Find the configuration robust to the step, not the one optimal before it.
goal: That setting rode out the change. Too few and you starve; too many and the upkeep eats you.
Robust to the step. The optimum sits between substrate limitation and maintenance cost — which is why cells regulate mitochondrial number rather than maximising it.

t: The power plants are called mitochondria. The energy they make is called ATP.
Those power plants are mitochondria, and the energy they make is a molecule called ATP.
Mitochondria carry out oxidative phosphorylation, converting glucose and oxygen into ATP — the molecule almost every process in the cell spends.
Mitochondria couple substrate oxidation to a proton gradient and use it to phosphorylate ADP. ATP is the universal intermediate, not the store.
sub: Here is the strange bit: mitochondria are about the size of a whole bacterium.
Here is the strange bit: a mitochondrion is about the size of a bacterium — and it has its own DNA.
Mitochondria are bacterium-sized, have their own circular DNA and divide independently. That is not a coincidence.
Bacterium-sized, circular genome, own ribosomes, binary fission. Endosymbiosis is the only hypothesis that accounts for all four.

t: When your muscles ache after running, that is your energy supply falling behind.
Trained athletes have more mitochondria in their muscles. That is a large part of what training actually changes.

Endurance training increases mitochondrial density; that adaptation, not muscle size, sets aerobic capacity. Mitochondrial disease presents first in the most energy-hungry tissues: heart, brain, muscle.
Mitochondrial myopathies track tissue ATP demand, which is why cardiac and neural presentation dominates. The same logic drives ischaemic injury timelines.

q: Why does the energy bar never stay still?
Why did the energy level never sit still, even when it was working?
Why is ATP level always changing even at steady state?
Why is a constant ATP pool not evidence of a static system?
options: Because energy is being made and spent all the time
Because the cell stores energy up
why: The cell never fills up. It makes energy and spends it at the same time, all the time.
There is no tank. Production and consumption run simultaneously, so the level is always the difference between two flows.
Steady state is a balance of two large opposing fluxes, not the absence of change. Stop synthesis and the pool is gone in seconds.
A constant pool reflects matched synthesis and hydrolysis rates, both large. Turnover, not stock, is the quantity that matters.

q: Why is building loads of power plants a bad idea?
Why did adding more and more power plants stop helping?
Why does mitochondrial number have an optimum rather than a maximum?
What sets the upper bound on useful mitochondrial density?
options: Each one costs energy to run
They get in each other's way
why: Every power plant needs energy just to keep going. Build too many and they eat more than they make.
Each mitochondrion has a maintenance cost. Past a point, the upkeep of the extras exceeds what they contribute.
Maintenance cost scales with number while output is capped by substrate supply, so net gain turns negative — cells regulate density rather than maximising it.
Output saturates at substrate limitation while maintenance scales linearly, so net ATP is non-monotonic in copy number.
